attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post, not a quote of anyone else.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'as far as I know' qualifier. 'After promising to collaborate' comes from the surrounding context. It is a qualified factual assertion, not a probability hedge, so it is an observation.

contract.note: Testing whether substantive work with Durbin actually happened is a fair plain reading. The open questions (whether written QFR answers count, whether staff work counts) are interpretations the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: Hearing transcript showing Altman's offer to collaborate. It says nothing about what happened afterwards.

Unofficial secondary transcription of post-hearing written answers about liability frameworks. Not checked against the primary record, and not shown to be work with Durbin. It neither proves nor rules out collaboration.

reviews.rationale: The packet has neither a comprehensive record showing no collaboration nor any authenticated record of substantive work with Durbin. The only possible follow-up (e2) is generic written answers whose primary source could not be read. The evidence does not settle the outcome.

attribution.note: Marcus's own footnote in his post.

semantics.note: Captures the three alleged lies. It drops the 'have control' part of the creator promise and the YC/fund details, but the contract restores them. The proposition is substantially faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'lies' as knowing falsity or deliberately misleading omission is the ordinary meaning. Requiring evidence about intent at the time for each component is fair. How the financial component scores depends on whether indirect exposure counts.

evidence.note: Transcript records what was said under oath ('no equity'), but not whether it was knowingly false.
Courtroom reporting (May 2026) of Altman admitting YC LP exposure he did not mention to the Senate. Supports the omission premise only; it does not establish deliberate deception.
Reuters report on Altman's Startup Fund ownership; OpenAI's denial of financial benefit is an interested statement. Does not settle personal interest at the hearing.
Shutterstock company disclosure of a pre-hearing compensation deal. Weighs against reading the compensation talk as insincere but does not settle it.
OpenAI lobbied to weaken specific EU rules. That does not show its stated support for regulation in general was false.

reviews.rationale: Only the factual premise of the financial omission has support (e2). Knowing falsity is not established for any of the three components, and none is affirmatively refuted. Under the contract that is neither support nor a mixed result.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. The quoted bill description is borrowed from WIRED, but he asserts it as his own claim.

semantics.note: Keeps 'would shield' (a proposed bill) and attributes 'pretty much the opposite' to Marcus as his characterization. The checkable core is OpenAI's support for SB3444.

contract.note: Reading 'state law' as a proposed bill and 'recently' as 2026 is fair and ordinary. Scoring only the legislative fact and leaving the evaluative comparison aside is appropriate.

evidence.note: CBS Chicago, May 2026: describes SB3444's shield for harms to 100+ people or $1B in damage, and reports that OpenAI supports it.
WIRED, Apr 2026: OpenAI testified for SB3444. Gives the thresholds and conditions (no intentional or reckless conduct, published safety reports).
In May 2026 OpenAI disavowed the safe harbor but confirmed it had testified in support of SB3444. Marcus omits this, but the bill support still happened.
Senate record of the 2023 testimony, relevant only to the evaluative comparison. Outside the target period.

reviews.rationale: Two independent news reports show OpenAI supported SB3444 in April–May 2026, a bill with conditional liability protection at the stated thresholds. OpenAI's later disavowal of the safe harbor qualifies but does not erase that support. The 'opposite/lie-filled' characterization is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'essentially all', 'fairly regularly', and the 'sometimes' harms. A general tendency claim about LLM providers' software.

contract.note: Reading it as a reproducible tendency across major providers, with no invented frequency threshold and an ordinary sense of 'defame', is fair. Choosing the 2026 pre-publication period is a reasonable evaluator decision.

evidence.note: HalluHard (Feb 2026) finds high hallucination rates across proprietary and open models, but on difficult multi-turn tasks rather than ordinary use.
AAAI Mar 2026 medical benchmark: every model makes clinically relevant errors (best 29.1%). The tests are adversarial traps and the experiments are undated. Supports the medical component.
Walters case (2023) fabricated an accusation, and the 2026 suits are only allegations. Too old, or unproven, to show defamatory output during the target period.
Same paper: rates vary by model and capability. This limits extrapolating to ordinary-use frequency but does not refute recurring fabrication.

reviews.rationale: 2026 benchmarks show fabrication across providers on hard tasks, and medical errors on adversarial clinical tests. The packet does not establish ordinary-use frequency, and has no authenticated reputational falsehoods from the target period. Nothing refutes the claim, but the contract's support condition is not met.
